body.p: Three hundred years ago there live an Evenk, with the name Choro. When he was newborn(?), the strong man Opchokon killed his mother and his father. He was left behind with the grandfather. The strong man Opchokon defeated several camps. The strong men compared they bows first, then they started shooting at each other from the distance of some steps, after having agreed on it. On their backs they had a quiver. In these quivers there were two or three hundred arrows. If they didn't hit each other, until the arrows had run out, they reconciled. When the child became big, the grandfather started teaching him to dodge [the arrows]. First he threw glowing coals at the child. The child jumped away from the heat of the fire. When he had [learned] to dodge the coal, [the grandfather] put glowing coals on the end of the arrow, he started shooting them. When [the son had learned] to dodge, he started shooting with an arrow, he was not immediately able to hit with it. Then he was seven years old. In the eighth year he followed Opchokon's marks. The grandfather told where they are living. Choro promised his father to come within seven days; if he doesn't come within seven days, that one should not wait. When three days had passed, he reached twenty tent: "Who has killed my father and my mother here, shall came out!" Opchokon said: "You hang up your head in vain". Choro said: "We'll look now, who [of us] will win". Opchokon said: "Who begins?" "You start, [you're] older!" Opchokon show three arrows in a row, Choro dodged. Choro said: "Was it the last one?" "Yes, the last one". Then it was Choro's turn to shoot. He shot once, into the navel, the second one into the heart, the third one into the forehead. Choro killed all, only two women he kept for himself as wives; he took all reindeer, all their belongings. Going around so he took four women. Then he got seven women. He became rich, he had workers, he was the master. From the seven women he had seven sons: The first was Kundogir, the second was Pangarakaj, the third was Mongo, the fourth was Hachakagir, the fifth was Hichogir, the sixth was Oluwul, the seventh was Putugir. From those seven boys the Evenks at the river Katonga arose. Choro went to hunt bears and took along his axe as well as his spear weighing fifteen pounds. He approached a bear lair and put the spear on top of a chopped birch. Not being afraid he came to the bear lair. When the bears arrived, he stabbed them with the spear one by one (?). Somewhere in his vicinity there lived five relatives. Ten ogres came to these relatives and said: "Let's play, we have a very good toy". They came, their toy was there (?). The toys is made out of shammy, it is closed and clad. The ogres creeped in and out and made noise. When the ogres came out, Choros relatives creeped in. They smashed all of them, only one small boy was left behind. Having slain [all] they wandered further along Choro's way. They made the boy to scout the path. At an obstacle he ran away (?). Going the [whole] night he caught up Choro. He told about the murder of the relatives. The ogres came to Choro, they said: "Let's play!" Choro said: "Fine, let's play!" They came to the playground. Choro said: "Who of you knows it, show how one has to play!" All ogres creeped in, Choro asked the ogres: "What does one do with the edging?" "One has to pull it!" Choro pulled, he smashed all of them; the boy chopped and said: "So you have smashed the parents". Then Choro wandered closer to a mountain called Natayo. When he was living there, a strong man from the Angara came, he started asking Choro for beasts. Choro pointed at the top of the [mountain] Natayo. In the morning they went off together. Then Choro had become old. When they were climbing onto the top of [the mountain] Natajo, Choro said: "Guys [= bears] have left a fresh trace". Having said he cut off a thick birch and knocked it into his spear. Going they saw eighteen bears. His friend stayed back. Choro went to the bears and said: "One by one, guys". He threw spears through the heads of the [bears] coming towards him. Piercing them he killed all of them. He looked for his friend, that one is nowhere, he has run away, his traces are hardly visible. Choro flayed [the bears] for three days. In the evening his friend came [to the camp] and said: "[Choro] climbed into a group of bears, where he can stand it (?)".[DCh]: The sense of the last clause is unclear. There his sons made arrows and said: "They ate our father, we'll show them". For that his relatives got to know that he is alive, on the fourth day Choro tied the claws of the biggest bear to his dog's neck, like a bell, and said: "Go". He himself arrived in the evening. He came to the bonfire, being angry at his friend. In the morning Choro said: "That man shall pull [it], [he] knows about it". They pulled and brought [the bears' carcasses]. In the evening they cooked them. They called Choro, that one didn't come. After they had eaten, Choro came, he saw the big head of a bear in the kettle, he pulled out his knife, he stabbed it [into the head] and threw it [= the head] to the dog. As reconciliation the Angara people gave their daughter to Choro's son.
